prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form that enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings placed B028 first, which I treat as a coincidence of independent judgments rather than as merit in itself. On the science, GLP-1 is a complete arc: proglucagon processing, identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, its glucose-dependent insulinotropic action, the extra-pancreatic effects on appetite, gut and heart, and then drugs whose benefit has been confirmed in large independent randomised trials in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal outcomes. The mechanism is stable, the clinical effect is large and still growing, and the recognition is timely. Holst (human GLP-1 physiology), Drucker (GLP-1 and GLP-2 biology and the gut-hormone axis) and Mojsov (the active peptide form) cover the discovery side as cleanly as three names allow, and a single achievement avoids splitting a prize across areas with weaker claims.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Credit for identifying the active GLP-1 peptide is contested between Mojsov and the Habener group, and Habener is not among the credited names, so any three-name set rests on a disputed priority judgement. The credited list also contains Knudsen, whose liraglutide and semaglutide work is what made the biology a medicine at scale. Omitting her could be read as honouring physiology while ignoring the step that changed patients' lives. A secondary concern is that long-term safety and secondary indications are still being defined.

responses.point: Linnarsson would credit Drucker, Holst and Knudsen: Holst and Drucker made the decisive physiological discoveries, and Knudsen led the translational design of long-acting analogues, while Mojsov's role is real but contested.
responses.response: I take the argument for Knudsen seriously, since without long-acting analogues the physiology would not have become a medicine. But the question I weigh is which contributions are discoveries and which are engineering on an established target. Mojsov's identification of the active peptide is a discovery-level step on which the later pharmacology depended. I do not think that a contested priority claim makes it less discovery-like than medicinal chemistry. I would put Knudsen first among the people I would reconsider if the committee decides the prize should honour development, but I would not drop the peptide-identification step to make room for her. I do not accept that the contested credit means Mojsov should be set aside; it means we must check the evidence carefully.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranks CAR-T second with June, Sadelain and Rosenberg, and raises whether an industry-based laureate fits the B028 configuration.
responses.response: On the industry point, I do not think the prize rule or precedent excludes industry scientists, so the objection should be about the nature of the contribution, not the employer. On CAR-T I disagree with adding Rosenberg. His adoptive cell transfer and early gene-modified T-cell trials are a distinct line, and adding him dilutes the costimulated-CAR story that Sadelain and June carried to clinical success. I would support a June and Sadelain pair as the clean version of B045, with the Eshhar gap noted. I think that this makes B045 a strong alternative but still behind B028 on completeness of the discovery chain.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius places cGAS-STING fourth and stresses its relevance to interferon-driven autoimmunity, with Chen and Barber as the cleanest pairing.
responses.response: I agree that Chen for cGAS and cGAMP and Barber for STING is the most defensible pairing, and the pathway is confirmed by many groups and structures. My reservation is maturity for this prize: STING was found near-simultaneously by several groups, the cyclic-dinucleotide biochemistry of Vance, Patel and others lies outside the credited names, and the clinical benefit of STING agonists or inhibitors is not yet shown. A good basic discovery, but I would not put it ahead of the incretin or CAR-T cases this year. I would revisit it if the committee wants a mechanistic immunology award rather than a therapeutic one.

responses.point: El-Manira ranks the unfolded protein response second and optogenetics third, with Walter and Mori as the natural pair for UPR and a Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann trio for optogenetics.
responses.response: I share the view that Walter and Mori are a clean pair for the unfolded protein response and it is among the most conceptually original cases on the list, which is why it is my alternative. For optogenetics I disagree on how well it fits: with six credited names and genuinely contested priority between channel discovery and neuronal application, any trio excludes someone whose contribution is widely regarded as decisive, and it is a method more than a discovery about disease. I would not combine it with B028 as a second part.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution to identifying the active GLP-1 peptide can be credited without crediting Habener, who is outside the supplied names.
Whether the committee prefers to honour the physiology (Drucker, Holst, Mojsov) or to include the drug-development step (Knudsen) in place of one of them.
Whether a second achievement (CAR-T or the unfolded protein response) should share the prize, which the three-person limit makes difficult given that B028 already needs three names.
My account of the credit history is from recollection and not independently verified against the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate on the shortlist has a specific connection to me apparent from my profile. I have co-authored work with committee colleagues Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisén and share Karolinska Institutet with other members, but none of this involves a shortlisted candidate, and I do not infer a personal tie from it.
